# Overview

This chapter describes the experimental methodology used to evaluate **Retrieval-Augmented Prediction (RAP)**, a test-time context-construction strategy for in-context-learning (ICL) tabular foundation models (FTMs) applied to fraud detection under heavy class imbalance. The chapter is organised around the components that together define a reproducible experiment: the problem formulation (@sec-problem), the datasets and their preprocessing (@sec-data), the splitting and test-set sampling protocol (@sec-protocol), the models under comparison (@sec-models), the context-construction conditions that operationalise RAP (@sec-conditions), the evaluation metrics (@sec-metrics), the full experimental grid (@sec-grid), and the implementation and reproducibility infrastructure (@sec-repro).

The design follows a controlled-ablation logic. Each research question maps to a comparison between two conditions that differ in exactly one factor, so that an observed difference in performance can be attributed to that factor alone. The conditions form a chain — random context, ratio-balanced context, retrieved context, and retrieved-plus-balanced context — that isolates first the effect of class-ratio control and then the effect of retrieval relevance.

# Problem formulation {#sec-problem}

Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN [@hollmann2025accurate_tabular_foundation_model; @hollmann2023tabpfn] and TabICL [@qu2026tabiclv2] perform classification by in-context learning: rather than fitting parameters by gradient descent, they take a labelled *context* (a set of training rows and their labels) together with a set of query rows, and produce predictions in a single forward pass. This builds on the prior-fitted-network framework, in which a transformer is meta-trained to approximate Bayesian inference over a prior of synthetic datasets [@muller2022transformers_bayesian_inference]. A practical consequence is a bounded context budget: the model was meta-trained over datasets up to a certain size, and inference quality and memory cost degrade outside that range. The context limits used in this work are reported in @sec-models.

Under heavy class imbalance the context budget becomes the central difficulty. When the positive (fraud) rate is on the order of $0.1$–$1\%$, a context drawn uniformly at random from the training set contains almost no positive examples — at a $0.17\%$ fraud rate, a $10{,}000$-row context is expected to hold roughly $17$ fraud rows, and at the per-batch level many contexts may contain none. The model is then asked to characterise the minority class from a handful of examples, or none at all.

RAP addresses this at **test time**, leaving the pre-trained model untouched. For each test batch it constructs a context that is (i) *relevant* — retrieved by nearest-neighbour search around the batch so the context resembles the queries — and (ii) *label-balanced* — oversampled to a controlled fraud ratio so the minority class is adequately represented. The research questions decompose these two effects:

| RQ | Question | Comparison |
|----|----------|------------|
| RQ1 | How do FTMs compare to GBDTs under naive random subsampling? | C1: FTM vs GBDT |
| RQ2 | Does random-subsample performance degrade as dataset size grows? | C1 across size tiers |
| RQ3 | Does retrieval-based context improve over random subsampling? | C3 vs C1 |
| RQ4 | What is the effect of the in-context fraud ratio? | C2 vs C1; C4 ratio sweep |

: Research questions and the condition comparisons that answer them. {#tbl-rq}

# Datasets {#sec-data}

## Selection and characteristics

Six publicly available transaction datasets form the **formal grid**, chosen to span fraud-detection settings while holding the supervised binary-classification task fixed. They vary along two axes that matter for the imbalance hypothesis: dataset size (from $\sim\!285$k to $6.3$M rows) and fraud prevalence ($0.13\%$ to $1.5\%$). A seventh dataset, AI Banking 2025, is used for pipeline development only and never enters the reported results: at a $28\%$ fraud rate it is nearly balanced and therefore unsuitable as an imbalance benchmark.

| Dataset | Rows | Features | Fraud % | Source | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| eu_cc (ULB) | 284,807 | 30 | 0.17% | Kaggle ULB credit-card | Formal grid |
| cc_2025 | 500,000 | 11 | 1.5% | Synthetic | Formal grid (degenerate) |
| banksim | 594,643 | 7 | 1.2% | BankSim simulator [@patil2024graphdb_banksim] | Formal grid |
| paysim | 6,362,620 | 7 | 0.13% | PaySim simulator [@alumona2025paysim_ml] | Formal grid |
| fifar | 602,961 | 29 | 1.2% | FiFAR [@alves2023fifar_learning_to_defer] | Formal grid |
| baf | 1,000,000 | 30 | 1.1% | Bank Account Fraud [@jesus2022baf_arxiv] | Formal grid |
| ai_banking | 10,000 | 6 | 28.4% | Synthetic | Dev only |

: Datasets. Full provenance and exploratory analysis appear in the companion data documentation. {#tbl-datasets}

Two datasets require explicit caveats that the thesis must state rather than bury:

- **cc_2025 is degenerate.** Its fraud labels are statistically independent of every feature: the distributions of `Amount`, `Distance`, `Is_International` and the remaining columns are identical for fraud and non-fraud rows. Consequently every model — FTM and GBDT alike — scores PR-AUC $\approx$ the fraud rate ($0.015$) and ROC-AUC $\approx 0.50$, i.e. random-chance performance. It is retained in the results not as a benchmark but as a documented example of a poorly constructed synthetic dataset; no further runs are queued for it beyond the C1/C2 results already collected.
- **BankSim contains entity identifiers.** The `customer` column is an entity ID ($\sim\!4{,}100$ customers over $594$k rows); its split treatment is discussed in @sec-protocol.

## Preprocessing

All datasets are ingested into a single local DuckDB database; the loader returns feature matrices and binary labels as NumPy arrays. Preprocessing is deliberately minimal and uniform:

- **Identifier and leakage columns are dropped** per dataset (e.g. account-name columns in PaySim, the post-hoc `isFlaggedFraud` flag, zip codes in BankSim, analyst-decision and model-score columns in FiFAR).
- **Categorical columns are ordinal-encoded** to integer codes; the FTMs and GBDTs both consume integer-coded categoricals.
- **Features are returned unscaled.** Tree-based GBDTs are scale-invariant, and FTM context rows are passed unscaled. Standardisation is applied *only* to build the nearest-neighbour index for retrieval (C3/C4); see @sec-conditions.
- **Time columns are kept as features.** `Time` (eu_cc) and `step` (BankSim, PaySim) are retained under the random split rather than dropped or used to define the split. This is a deliberate choice — under a random split they carry weak signal and removing them would discard information available at prediction time — and the temporal-generalisation question is instead handled as a separate ablation (@sec-protocol).

# Splitting and evaluation protocol {#sec-protocol}

## Train/test split

The default split is a seeded, stratified $80/20$ train/test partition, with two principled exceptions:

- **BankSim uses a grouped split by `customer`.** Because `customer` is an encoded entity ID and the same customer appears in many rows, a row-level random split would place a customer's transactions on both sides of the partition; the model could then memorise the customer code as a near-perfect label key, inflating test performance through leakage. A `GroupShuffleSplit` instead assigns each customer wholly to train or to test. Grouped splits are not label-stratified, but with thousands of groups the fraud rate stays close to the population rate.
- **FiFAR uses its published fixed split.** Because the split is predetermined, the random seed has no effect, so FiFAR is run once rather than three times.

## Test-set negative subsampling

Prediction cost for the FTMs scales with the number of test rows, and on the larger datasets the full test set dominates wall-clock time. Because the positive class is small and drives metric variance, the protocol keeps **all** test positives and randomly downsamples test negatives to a per-dataset cap (`test_neg_cap`, default $30{,}000$; eu_cc is exempt and always scored in full, as it has only $\sim\!98$ test frauds for which rare-event metrics would be indefensible under subsampling). The subsample is deterministic in the run seed and independent of the context-construction RNG stream.

Subsampling negatives changes the empirical class prevalence, which would bias precision-based metrics upward. Two facts make this correctable. First, the ROC quantities (true-positive and false-positive rates) are invariant to random negative subsampling, so Recall@FPR and ROC-AUC are unaffected. Second, precision at any threshold can be recomputed at the *true* (full-split) prevalence $\pi$ from the ROC quantities,

$$
\text{precision}(t) = \frac{\pi \cdot \mathrm{TPR}(t)}{\pi \cdot \mathrm{TPR}(t) + (1-\pi)\cdot \mathrm{FPR}(t)},
$$

and the prevalence-corrected average precision is obtained by integrating precision over recall along the score-sorted thresholds. At $\pi$ equal to the observed prevalence this reduces to the standard average precision to machine precision, so the corrected estimator is used uniformly and is exact when no subsampling occurs.

## Temporal generalisation (ablation)

The main grid uses random splits and keeps time as a feature. The orthogonal question of temporal generalisation — training on the past and testing on the future — is handled as a dedicated ablation rather than folded into the main grid. The natural vehicle is BAF, whose published protocol splits by `month` (already excluded as a feature); this isolates the effect of distribution shift without confounding it with the main comparisons. [TODO: finalise the temporal-ablation design and report.]

## Repetitions

Each configuration is run under three seeds (42, 123, 7), except FiFAR (fixed split, one run). Results are aggregated as mean $\pm$ standard deviation across seeds; FiFAR is reported as a single point estimate.

# Models {#sec-models}

## Tabular foundation models

Five ICL tabular foundation models are evaluated, spanning the current TabPFN line and an independent architecture (TabICL):

| Key | Model | Context limit (rows × features) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tabpfn_v2` | TabPFN v2 | 10,000 × 500 | Ungated [@hollmann2025accurate_tabular_foundation_model] |
| `tabpfn_25` | TabPFN 2.5 | 50,000 × 2,000 | Gated; license accepted [@grinsztajn2025tabpfn25_arxiv] |
| `tabpfn_26` | TabPFN 2.6 | 50,000 × 2,000 | Gated; license accepted |
| `tabpfn_3` | TabPFN v3 | 50,000 × 2,000 | Gated; license acceptance pending [TODO] |
| `tabiclv2` | TabICLv2 | ~48,000 × 500 | BSD-3 [@qu2026tabiclv2] |

: Foundation models and their context budgets. Limits are soft, based on the pre-training size range. {#tbl-ftms}

All FTMs run on GPU (`device="cuda"`, NVIDIA RTX 5070) through a common wrapper exposing the scikit-learn `fit` / `predict_proba` interface, where `fit` loads the context rather than training weights. The `tabpfn` library version is 8.0.8 and `tabicl` is 2.0.3; both versions are recorded per run for provenance.

::: {.callout-note}
At time of writing, TabPFN v3 weights require a one-time license acceptance for the account holding the API token; until that is granted, `tabpfn_3` is excluded from the run driver and the in-flight grid is effectively four FTMs. The model is included in the target design and back-filled once the license is accepted.
:::

## GBDT baselines

XGBoost [@chen2016xgboost_scalable_tree_boosting] and CatBoost [TODO: cite] serve as reference points. Both are class-weighted (`scale_pos_weight = n_neg / n_pos`) and otherwise use library defaults — they are reference baselines, not the object of study.

Crucially, **GBDTs are trained on the full training set and run only under condition C1.** The bounded context window is an inherent property of the FTMs being evaluated, not a constraint to impose on every model. The FTM-versus-GBDT comparison therefore measures how an ICL model performs under its architectural data limitation against a model that sees all available training data — which is the practically relevant question.

# Context-construction conditions {#sec-conditions}

The four conditions differ only in how the FTM context is assembled; the model, split, and evaluation are held fixed.

| ID | Name | Context construction | Fraud ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | Random | Uniform random subsample to the context limit | Natural |
| C2 | Stratified | Class-balanced subsample | 50/50 |
| C3 | kNN (control) | Nearest-neighbour retrieval around the test batch | Natural |
| C4 | RAP | kNN retrieval + controlled fraud oversampling | Swept: 5/10/20/30/50% |

: Context-construction conditions. {#tbl-conditions}

**C1 (random)** is the naive baseline: a single context of `min(n_train, context_limit)` rows sampled uniformly, reused for all test rows. **C2 (stratified)** balances the context to 50/50 (taking all available fraud if fewer than half the budget); comparing C2 with C1 isolates the effect of class ratio with relevance held constant. **C3 (kNN control)** retrieves, for each test batch, the $k$ nearest training rows to the batch centroid in standardised feature space, at the natural fraud ratio; C3 versus C1 isolates the effect of relevance. **C4 (RAP)** combines retrieval with controlled oversampling of the fraud quota; C4 versus C3 isolates the effect of ratio tuning on top of retrieval, and the ratio sweep answers RQ4.

For C1 and C2 the context is built once and reused, so prediction over the test set can be chunked purely for GPU-memory reasons without affecting results. For C3 and C4 the context is rebuilt per batch around that batch's centroid.

## RAP pipeline {#sec-rap}

The retrieval pipeline (Phase 3 implementation; the conditions above are specified, the modules are in progress) comprises three stages:

1. **Retriever.** A nearest-neighbour index is built on **standardised** training features (a `StandardScaler` fit on the training split only). Distance metric (cosine vs Euclidean) is chosen empirically on the development dataset. The standardisation is used solely to make distances comparable across features; the context rows handed to the FTM remain unscaled.
2. **Sampler.** Given the retrieved candidate pool and a target fraud ratio, the sampler fills the fraud quota — drawing from the global fraud pool, and **with replacement** (duplicating fraud rows) when unique training fraud is exhausted. Oversampling is the method under study, so the quota is filled rather than capped at the available unique fraud; a run records both `context_fraud_n` and `context_fraud_unique` so the duplication factor is recoverable, and duplication-heavy cells are annotated or excluded at analysis time against a stated threshold rather than dropped from the grid.
3. **Context builder.** Assembles the final `(X_ctx, y_ctx)` for the condition and dispatches to the model.

Two guards apply. Retrieval batches are formed from homogeneous groups of test rows (clustering/sorting in feature space) so that each batch centroid is representative. And C3 must guard against fraud-free retrieved contexts, since a single-class context breaks `predict_proba(...)[:, 1]`. [TODO: finalise guard behaviour when implementing `src/rap/`.]

# Evaluation metrics {#sec-metrics}

Performance is reported with metrics appropriate to heavy imbalance, where accuracy and unqualified ROC-AUC are misleading.

- **PR-AUC (average precision)** is the primary metric, computed prevalence-corrected as described in @sec-protocol so that test-set subsampling introduces no bias.
- **Recall@1%FPR** and **Recall@5%FPR** report the true-positive rate achievable at a fixed false-positive budget — directly meaningful for fraud screening, where operating points are chosen by the cost of investigating false alarms. These use the **conservative step-function value** of the empirical ROC curve: the highest TPR among operating points with $\mathrm{FPR} \le$ target. Linear interpolation between ROC points is deliberately avoided, because interpolated $(\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{TPR})$ pairs do not correspond to any achievable decision threshold and therefore overestimate recall — a bias that is pronounced when the positive class is small and the empirical curve is coarse (e.g. eu_cc, with $\sim\!100$ test frauds). The step value carries a small downward bias of one negative-count step ($1/N_\text{neg}$), negligible at $N \approx 30$k.
- **ROC-AUC** and **F1** (at threshold $0.5$) are reported as secondary metrics.

# Experimental grid {#sec-grid}

The full grid spans datasets, models, conditions, and seeds:

- **Dataset–seed units:** $5$ datasets $\times\,3$ seeds $+$ FiFAR $\times\,1 = 16$.
- **FTM core:** $5$ models $\times\,4$ conditions $\times\,16 = 320$ runs.
- **GBDT core:** $2$ models $\times\,1$ condition $\times\,16 = 32$ runs.
- **C4 fraud-ratio sweep:** $5$ FTMs $\times\,5$ ratios $\times\,16 = 320$ net-new runs (the default-ratio C4 point is shared with the core).
- **Batch-size sweep:** $1$ FTM $\times\,4$ sizes $\times\,2$ datasets $\times\,3$ seeds $= 24$ runs.

cc_2025 cells beyond the already-collected C1/C2 results are dropped (degenerate, @sec-data).

## Ensemble passes

Each FTM prediction averages over `n_estimators` ensemble passes (input/feature permutations). The library default is $8$; reducing it speeds prediction roughly linearly but changes outputs. **All reported FTM results use `n_estimators = 4`**, chosen to keep the full grid tractable on a single GPU; the runner default of $8$ is retained only for ad-hoc single runs. The value is recorded per run, so the setting is auditable and runs are never mixed across values.

# Implementation and reproducibility {#sec-repro}

The experiment harness is built for exact reproducibility and safe restartability.

- **Language split.** Python handles all model training, inference, and the RAP pipeline; R + Quarto + Typst handle analysis, tables, figures, and this document. The two communicate only through Parquet files written to `results/runs/` — no in-process bridge.
- **Determinism.** All randomness flows through `numpy.random.default_rng(seed)`; the test-subsampling stream is offset (`seed ^ 0x5CA1E`) to stay independent of context construction. Library versions are pinned via `uv` and `uv.lock`.
- **Idempotent runner.** Each run is fully specified by a configuration dict whose canonical serialisation is SHA-256 hashed to a `run_id` and output path; an existing file is skipped. Runs can be killed and restarted without recomputation or duplication.
- **Pipeline versioning.** A `_PIPELINE_VERSION` integer is part of the config hash. Any change to model defaults or pipeline logic increments it, invalidating cached results so that a reported table never mixes incompatible pipeline behaviour. Results are filtered to the current version (4) for analysis.
- **Per-run provenance.** Each run records the full configuration, all metrics, true and scored test counts, context composition, library versions, and a three-way timing split (setup / fit / predict) so that one-time model-loading cost never contaminates fit/predict comparisons.

This produces, for every cell of the grid, a single self-describing Parquet row, from which all thesis tables and figures are derived.
